solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Nameless clarinetist perhaps performing in concert

indicators.note: Something nameless has lost its name, and N is the standard abbreviation for name, so the fodder drops its N.
Performers put on an act, so the letters are made to act out a new order.

blocks.note: the eleven letters of the musician with N (name) taken out

explanation.surface: An unnamed clarinet player giving a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the fodder: a clarinetist playing a concert is one example of the answer, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a solo player giving a recital, such as a clarinetist on stage, is a recitalist.

clue.text: Capital of two US states

blocks.note: the postal abbreviation for Rhode Island

explanation.surface: A trivia question about a city serving as seat of government for two American states.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for an American capital; the answer is a European one built from two postal abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Latvian seat of government is one of Europe's capital cities.

clue.text: Happen to turn round

blocks.note: the sailing sense: swing onto the other tack

explanation.surface: Someone who chances to turn and look behind them.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is nautical: a sailing boat comes about when it swings onto the other tack.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one phrasal verb: everyday 'occur', and the sailor's word for going about onto a new tack.

clue.text: Play awful when trite and no longer fresh

indicators.note: Something awful is in a terrible state, so the letters of 'when trite' are to be put in a different one.

explanation.surface: A drama critic panning a play as hackneyed and stale.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a bad review, which conceals that 'Play' is the definition and names one of Shakespeare's.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is one of Shakespeare's late plays.

clue.text: Weapon for which one keeps one’s head down a good while?

definitions.text: Weapon for which one keeps one’s head down a good while?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a weapon you use while ducking, as in a trench

blocks.clueFragment: keeps one’s head down a good while
blocks.note: the setter's reading: a head lowered for a lengthy time makes an extended bow

explanation.surface: A soldier keeping their head low for safety while using some weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the weapon's name as two words: a LONG BOW is what you make if you keep your head down a good while.
explanation.definitionFit: The weapon is the tall medieval English bow; the question mark flags the pun on bowing one's head.

clue.text: More than one cut, not quite every one

indicators.note: Something not quite complete falls just short, so the word for 'every one' loses its last letter.

blocks.note: ALL (every one) minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A remark that more than one got cut, though not all of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a single statement about cuts; 'More than one' is the definition and the rest builds it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: several means a number greater than one but not many.

clue.text: Nitrogen in cigarette that delivers poison

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun: the thing that delivers poison

indicators.note: Nitrogen is literally placed in the cigarette, so its symbol sits inside the slang word.

blocks.note: the chemical symbol, placed after FA

explanation.surface: A health warning about the toxic compounds in cigarette smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the cigarette the poisoner; the definition is the snake's tooth. A fag is British slang for a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a snake's hollow tooth is what injects its venom.

clue.text: Past river, a market

blocks.note: in the past, as in 'long ago'

explanation.surface: Directions: go past the river and you reach a market.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Past' as a preposition of place; it is the adverb of time.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical sense: the open square of an ancient Greek city served as its marketplace.

clue.text: With vegetables, pull up grass

indicators.note: In a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the word for 'pull' is written backwards.

blocks.note: as a horse draws a cart

explanation.surface: A gardener lifting vegetables and weeding the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull up' looks like a gardening phrase, but 'pull' is DRAW and 'up' turns it round in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary word: an expanse of grassy turf is what old writers called by this name.

clue.text: Leaving an unfinished task and settling down

indicators.note: An unfinished job lacks its ending, so the word for task loses its last letter.

blocks.note: abandoning, as in dropping a subject

explanation.surface: Someone abandoning a half-done job to put their feet up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one lazy action; 'Leaving an unfinished task' is all wordplay and 'settling down' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative use of a nautical phrase: a ship that stops and stays put has settled, as a person does.

clue.text: I want a little something immediately

indicators.note: A little of something is a small part of it, so the answer is a small part of the next two words.

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word and the first four of the second

explanation.surface: An impatient child demanding a treat right now.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a slurred 'give me', the very cry the surface is acting out.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial idiom: the slurred demand for something is how a grabby child says it wants it.

clue.text: Always behind rear of column: not again!

indicators.note: Behind means following on, so the word for always is placed after the letter.
The rear of a column is its tail end, so take the last letter of the word.

explanation.surface: A soldier stuck forever at the back of a marching column, vowing never again.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is the refrain of Poe's poem 'The Raven'.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary synonym: the exclamation means never again.

clue.text: Plausibly, rains ruined army training here

indicators.note: Something ruined is wrecked and must be rebuilt, so the letters are reassembled.

explanation.surface: An excuse that bad weather spoilt an army exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a large chalk plateau in Wiltshire, England, used by the British Army as its main training ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the British Army has trained on this Wiltshire plateau for over a century.

clue.text: Go canoeing for relaxation, but not in such a craft

definitions.note: the answer describes the craft: a canoe is not an ocean-going vessel

indicators.note: Relaxation is a loosening, and letters loosened up are free to settle in a new order.

explanation.surface: Advice to paddle a canoe for leisure, but to keep off the open sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For relaxation' reads as the reason to paddle; it is the anagram signal. The definition works by contrast: a canoe is no ship for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by contrast: a canoe is the opposite of a vessel built for the open sea.

clue.text: Native American chief’s first love arrested by guard taken back

indicators.note: The first of a word is its opening letter, so chief gives C.
Someone arrested is held by the police, so love is held inside the word for guard.
Taking something back returns it the way it came, so the guard with love inside is written backwards.

blocks.note: love = nil = O in tennis, placed between WATC and H

explanation.surface: A tribal chief's sweetheart seized by a sentry.
explanation.walkthrough: The chief's first letter stands outside the reversal; only WATCH with O inside it is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is one of the Native American peoples of the south-eastern United States.

clue.text: Look after youngster grabbing one whiskey that’s downed

indicators.note: After means coming later in order, so the word for look is placed after the boy.
Grabbing is taking hold of, so the youngster closes around the one.

blocks.note: W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Minding a young person who has drunk a whiskey and passed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look after' reads as 'take care of'; it is LO placed after the next piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: knocked down or brought low, as by illness or a blow.

clue.text: Stories about endlessly pompous rituals

indicators.note: About means around, so the word for stories goes around the other piece.
Without its end, the word for pompous loses its last letter.

blocks.note: fibs, as when a child tells stories

explanation.surface: Tall tales told around solemn ceremonies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stories' here are fibs, as in a child telling stories.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: set forms of public worship are religious rituals.

clue.text: Insects eating live one of the Scorpion group

indicators.note: Whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so the insects take the other piece in.

explanation.surface: Insects devouring a live scorpion.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scorpion group is the constellation Scorpius, not a family of creatures.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this red giant is the brightest star in the constellation of the Scorpion.

clue.text: Postponed decision about small particle

blocks.note: a subatomic particle such as the electron

explanation.surface: A physicist putting off a verdict on a tiny particle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' belongs to the definition: the phrase means putting off a decision about something overnight.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: if you sleep on a problem you delay deciding until the next day.

clue.text: Aircraft following large boat, heading off

indicators.note: A heading is what comes at the top, so taking it off removes the boat's first letter.

blocks.note: f. = following, as in page references
LIGHTER, a big flat-bottomed barge, without its first letter

explanation.surface: A plane tailing a big ship, then turning away.
explanation.walkthrough: A lighter is a barge used to ferry cargo to and from ships; FREIGHTER tempts, but it would need three letters off.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a fast military plane built for air combat is one kind of aircraft.

clue.text: Wrong order at first of rising problem in flock

indicators.note: What comes at first is at the very start, so order gives only its opening letter.
In a down entry, rising means reading upwards, so the assembled pieces are written backwards.

explanation.surface: A shepherd noticing that something is out of order in the flock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong order' looks like one phrase, but 'Wrong' is TORT alone and 'order' only lends its O.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: this hoof infection of sheep is a common trouble for a flock.

clue.text: Leave London, hoping to be returned?

blocks.note: head out of the city for rural parts
a British government calling a general election, hoping voters return it to office

explanation.surface: A Londoner off to the countryside, hoping to come back.
explanation.walkthrough: In British politics a prime minister calls a general election by this phrase, hoping to be returned to office.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a literal trip out of town, and the British idiom for putting a government before the voters.

clue.text: Delicious pie with a different crust

indicators.note: A crust is the outside of a pie, so the pie's outer letter at the front is changed.

blocks.note: a folded pastry pie, like the Cornish pasty

explanation.surface: A pie that tastes great because of a new pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: A pasty is a folded pastry pie with a savoury filling, a British staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: food that is pleasing to eat is both.

clue.text: Not straight, because bent

explanation.surface: Something called crooked because it is bent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' is a noun here, an inclination. 'Not straight' reads as a second definition but builds the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the noun: a bent is a natural leaning, as a bias is.

clue.text: Abuse involving American pair leading orchestra and conductor? Absolutely not

indicators.note: To involve is to take something in, so the word for abuse wraps round the American.
What leads is at the front, so the pair is the first two letters of orchestra.

blocks.note: the first two letters of orchestra

explanation.surface: A scandal about an American duo mistreating an orchestra and its conductor.
explanation.walkthrough: The orchestra and conductor are musical in the surface; the definition means an electrical conductor, of which the answer is the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by contrast: a material that blocks electric current is the opposite of a conductor.

clue.text: Hot island? One part of island

blocks.note: an ait is a small river island, as in the Thames

explanation.surface: A question whether an island is hot, answered with a geography lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: An ait (or eyot) is a British word for an islet in a river. The country shares Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic, which makes the definition fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: this country occupies the western third of the island of Hispaniola.

clue.text: Artist’s spiritual exercises transferring pieces in odd places

indicators.note: Pieces moved between the odd-numbered places swap round, so the first and third letters trade.

blocks.note: the Indian discipline of meditation and posture; Y and G, in places one and three, swap

explanation.surface: A painter's meditative routine with the props moved about.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the odd-numbered letters move: Y and G swap, O and A stay put.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Francisco Goya was a Spanish painter.

clue.text: One has confidence in investments

explanation.surface: An investor who believes in the stock market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like part of 'confidence in', but it joins wordplay to definition. A unit trust is the British name for a mutual fund.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: pooled funds are one kind of investment, the British counterpart of mutual funds.
